primary_bug.summary: withStreamIdleTimeout adds an idle watchdog that ACTIVELY DESTROYS the underlying stream (void stream.destroy()) when no network chunk arrives within SSE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS (60s), or SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS (2min) before the first chunk. But a gap longer than that occurs LEGITIMATELY during normal active generation — server-side tool execution, extended thinking, queueing, slow/long TTFT — so the watchdog terminates streams that are not actually hung. The consequence: live responses are truncated mid-flight, surfacing to users as 'Sorry, the response hit the length limit' with no actual output (regression issue #308627), which is why the ENTIRE feature was reverted the same day (#308779). Objective confirmation of the intended resolution: the eventual re-approach to the same hung-stream problem (#321671) is deliberately OBSERVE-ONLY — it arms an idle watchdog purely to emit telemetry and states verbatim 'It does not change request behavior — the stream is not aborted' — i.e., the accepted lesson is that actively aborting on an idle timeout (what this PR did) is unsafe.
primary_bug.locus: withStreamIdleTimeout (~L82-129 of the diff): startTimer() arms a setTimeout whose callback does `timedOut = true; void stream.destroy()`, armed around each `await iterator.next()`; SSE_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=60_000 / SSE_FIRST_CHUNK_TIMEOUT_MS=120_000. Applied at the 3 `for await (const chunk of withStreamIdleTimeout(...))` call sites.
primary_bug.must_flag: A reviewer catches the primary bug if it identifies that the watchdog can DESTROY / abort a stream that is still legitimately active — i.e., that treating a >60s (or >2min first-chunk) network-idle gap as 'hung' and tearing the stream down produces FALSE timeouts on live streams (legitimate long pauses during generation: tool calls, thinking, slow TTFT), truncating responses. Equivalent framings that count as TP-primary: 'the 60s idle threshold is too aggressive for LLM/SSE streams that legitimately pause and will kill live streams'; 'actively destroying the stream on idle is unsafe — a paused-but-alive stream is aborted, better to observe/measure than abort'; 'a long server-side gap (tool call / extended thinking) exceeds the timeout and terminates a healthy stream → truncated output'. The strongest catch names BOTH the active-destroy and the legitimacy of long gaps.
primary_bug.source: revert PR #308779 ('Revert "Support timing out hung streams (#308517)"', Fix #308627) + regression issue #308627 (user: 'response hit the length limit' but Copilot produced no output — truncated stream) + the accepted observe-only re-approach #321671 which explicitly does NOT abort the stream. Verified against the checkout at merge ba8d730: withStreamIdleTimeout's timer callback calls stream.destroy(); thresholds are 60s / 2min; wired into all three SSE consumers.
primary_bug.difficulty: HARD, and a deliberate trap. The code looks like the textbook idle-timeout anti-pattern, and a Copilot review bot on an EARLIER commit flagged exactly the 'timer measures consumer processing time' bug — but the author FIXED that before merge (see known_safe: clearTimer() is called immediately after await iterator.next() and BEFORE yield, with an explicit comment and a dedicated passing test 'consumer processing time longer than idle timeout does not cause false timeout'). So the merged code does NOT measure consumer time; a finding asserting it does is a FALSE POSITIVE (misreads the clearTimer-before-yield), NOT a catch. The real escaped defect is the more semantic one — active abort on an over-aggressive idle threshold kills legitimately-paused-but-live streams — which requires either domain knowledge that LLM streams legitimately pause >60s, or noticing the whole feature was reverted. Expect low true recall and a high rate of the M1 false positive, especially from tools that retrieved and parroted the bot comment without verifying it against the merged code.

known_safe.summary: The idle timer is cleared BEFORE each yield: the loop is startTimer() -> `await iterator.next()` -> clearTimer() -> yield. So the timer brackets ONLY the network read (`await iterator.next()`), NOT consumer processing (which happens while the generator is suspended at yield, timer disarmed). The diff carries an explicit comment ('Consumer processing time is NOT timed — the timer is cleared above') and a dedicated passing test ('consumer processing time longer than idle timeout does not cause false timeout') that advances fake time by 3x the idle timeout during consumer processing and asserts no timeout. Therefore any finding claiming the merged code 'starts/leaves the idle timer running during consumer processing', 'measures time between consumer next() calls / includes parsing time', or 'false-times-out under slow CONSUMERS' is a FALSE POSITIVE — it misreads the clearTimer-before-yield (this is precisely the earlier-commit bug the Copilot bot flagged, which the author fixed before merge). Note the distinction: false timeout on a slow NETWORK gap (legitimate generation pause) is the real primary bug; false timeout on a slow CONSUMER is refuted.

The timer callback is `void stream.destroy().catch(() => { })` — the destroy() promise's rejection IS explicitly handled/swallowed. Flagging an 'unhandled promise rejection on stream.destroy() in the timer path' is a false positive (this was a Copilot-bot comment on an earlier commit, addressed before merge).

The generator's `finally` calls `clearTimer(); await iterator.return?.();` — early consumer termination (break/return/throw) IS forwarded to the underlying stream iterator, releasing the reader lock. Flagging a 'reader-lock leak / missing iterator.return() on early break' is a false positive (also a Copilot-bot comment on an earlier commit, addressed before merge; there is a dedicated passing test 'consumer break releases the underlying reader lock').
